lesson.title: Drift or noise: trends over time

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the best-fit line still leaning a little, and a different way each time, when you drop fresh batches with no drift set.
interactive.title: Tip and peel
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This lesson runs over thirteen small screens. Each bead is one simulated reading of a battery bank's float voltage, taken on rounds. Say its charger holds it at 27.00 V. A rule on screen makes each reading. Call the reading's number i, counting from 0. Start at 27.00 V. Add the drift times i ÷ 10. Add the random error times the sum of twelve small nudges. Each nudge lies between minus a half and plus a half. Then round it to the meter's step of 0.01 V. Here the random error is 0.03 V. Fifty readings pour from the hopper through the peg field. They land on the beam, which balances on its fulcrum at the mean. Then they rise into a swarm, each bead at its own value. A dashed line marks the mean, with its value above it. A key under the picture says what each bead's colour means. Then the swarm tips onto its side. The readings peel off along a thread, in the order taken. The mean so far writes itself beside them. A flat line at the mean tilts into the best-fit line. That is the straight line that sits closest to all fifty. A tile, Trend per 10 readings, gives the line's slope. A slider, Drift per 10 readings, runs from 0 to 0.010 V in steps of 0.001 V and opens at 0. A tile, Longest run up or down, counts the most readings in a row that each read higher than the last, or each lower. A button, Drop a fresh batch, pours fifty new readings. Two more views come later. The first shows sixteen simulated insulation resistance tests on a pump motor's winding. There is one test each quarter for four years. They are drawn on a scale by factors. Say its resistance at 20 °C starts at 1000 MΩ. It falls by a factor of 10 to the power 0.02 each test, which is about 4.5%. Each test also scatters by a factor of 10 to the power 0.02 times its twelve nudges. Through each year, the tests are taken at 20, 30, 20 and 10 °C. As a rough rule of thumb, say the resistance halves for every 10 °C warmer. A choice offers As measured or Corrected to 20 °C. Corrected doubles a reading for each 10 °C its test sat above 20 °C. It halves a reading for each 10 °C below. The second view shows two strings of readings, taken every 4 hours over the same days. One is a pump bearing's temperature. The other is a battery's float current. Each day the air temperature swings round 25 °C. A slider, How much the air swings, runs from 0 to ±4 °C in steps of 0.5 °C and opens at ±3 °C. Say the bearing reads 40 °C. Add 0.8 °C for each degree the air sits above 25 °C. Add 0.5 °C times its own twelve nudges. Round it to 0.1 °C. Say the float current reads 0.4 A. Add 0.03 A for each degree the air sits above 25 °C. Add 0.02 A times twelve nudges of its own. Round it to 0.001 A. This rule is made up to show a shared cause. It claims nothing about real bearings or batteries. A choice, Show them, switches from Over time to One against the other. Folded, each pair becomes one point: the current against the bearing. A best-fit line runs through them. A tile, How closely they line up, runs from +1 for a perfect rising line, through 0 for none, to −1 for a perfect falling line. The screens. 1, show: fifty readings pour, land round 27.00 V and rise into a swarm. A swarm hides the order the readings came in. It tips onto its side. The readings peel off in the order taken. One reading on its own tells you little, because noise moves every reading. What matters is the trend over many. 2, a puzzle: the same fifty readings come in two different orders. In one they creep up steadily. In the other they jumble. What tells the two apart? Offered: plotting them in the order taken; their mean and standard deviation; and the shape of the swarm. Hint when wrong: the swarm and its numbers keep no record of the order. 3, show: a flat line at the mean tilts into the best-fit line. Its slope measures the drift per reading. The trend tile gives it per 10 readings. The line always passes through the mean point. That point sits at the mean reading number and the mean voltage. Slide the drift up, and the readings climb along the line. The finished picture shows a drift of 0.008 V per 10 readings, with the readings climbing along the line. 4, a puzzle: the trend tile reads +0.008 V per 10 readings. About how far does the line climb from the first reading to the fiftieth? Offered: about 0.04 V; 0.008 V; and 0.4 V. Hint: fifty readings span about five lots of 10. 5, show: set the drift to zero and drop fresh batches. The line still leans a little, a different way each time. Each batch's random errors happen to sit a little higher at one end. The line follows them, because it fits whatever readings it gets. That lean is noise. In this simulation, with no drift, 95 batches in 100 lean by less than about 0.006 V per 10 readings either way. A drift bigger than that noise leans the line the same way, batch after batch. The finished picture shows a fresh batch with no drift. Its line leans a little. 6, a puzzle: a fresh batch's trend tile reads +0.003 V per 10 readings. Noise alone leans the line by under about 0.006 V per 10 readings in 95 batches in 100. What does that show? Offered: nothing on its own, as noise alone leans the line that much now and then; the voltage drifts up 0.003 V per 10 readings; and the meter reads high. Hint: compare 0.003 with the 0.006 that noise alone can give. 7, show: the tile Longest run up or down counts the most readings in a row each higher than the last, or each lower. With pure noise, six readings can come in 720 orders, all equally likely. One climbs all the way and one falls. So a given six run one way about 1 time in 360. Fifty noisy readings here usually give a longest run of 3 to 5. A run needs a change per reading as big as the noise, as in the insulation tests ahead. Even the largest drift, 0.001 V a reading against 0.03 V of noise, is far smaller, so it shows only in the trend tile. 8, a puzzle: pure noise, four readings in a row. What is the chance they climb all the way? Offered: 1 in 24; 1 in 8, as each step up is a coin toss; and 1 in 4. Hint: four readings can come in 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 orders, and only one climbs. The steps are not separate coin tosses, because each shares a reading with the next. 9, show: now the beads are sixteen insulation resistance tests, on a scale by factors. As measured, they zigzag. Some test days were warmer, and warm insulation reads low. Choose Corrected to 20 °C, and the beads hop to their corrected places. Now a steady fall shows. The longest run down often reaches six or more. This string was picked to show one. Read the line only across the tests you have. Past the last one, it is a guess. The finished picture shows the corrected string falling, with its best-fit line. 10, a puzzle: a winding tested at 30 °C reads 300 MΩ. Using the rule of thumb, what does it read corrected to 20 °C? Offered: 600 MΩ; 150 MΩ; and 300 MΩ. Hint: at 20 °C the winding is 10 °C cooler. Cooler insulation reads higher, so double it. 11, show: two strings over the same days, a pump bearing's temperature and a battery's float current. The air swings ±3 °C each day. The rule makes both follow it. Over time they rise and fall together. Choose One against the other, and each pair folds into one point. The points line up closely, near 0.9 on the tile. Yet neither drives the other. The air drives both. Set the air steady, and they make a round cloud. The finished picture shows the folded pairs lining up along their best-fit line. 12, a mixed puzzle: a winding's insulation resistance and its temperature line up closely in your records. How could you show that warmth lowers the resistance? Offered: test one winding at two temperatures, with everything else kept the same; you cannot, because correlation never shows cause; and gather more records until they line up even more closely. Hint: change one thing yourself and watch. A shared cause cannot explain a change you made. 13, a mixed puzzle: corrected to 20 °C, a motor's last six tests each read lower than the one before. Every reading still passes its minimum. What do you make of it? Offered: a steady fall, rare by chance, so look into it now; nothing, as every reading passes; and run the line on to find the day it reaches the minimum. Hint: six in a row one way is rare from noise alone. A reading can pass and still be part of a fall. The trend shows where it is heading. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. On a narrow phone, the tiles and answers wrap onto more lines. No word splits.
interactive.ignores: The readings are simulated from the rules on screen, not taken from real equipment. The float voltage, the random error, the drifts, the insulation resistance, the test temperatures and the bearing and current rules are all examples. A real drift is rarely a perfect straight line. It can speed up, level off or jump. Equal readings break a run here, so runs come a little shorter than the count of orders suggests. Real insulation follows the halving rule only roughly. Here correcting removes the temperature exactly, because the same rule made the readings. Real readings taken close together can also share noise, such as one warm week. That makes leans and runs more common than here.

explain.text:
Plot readings in the order you took them, and you can tell a slow change from the wobble every reading has. A [[drift]] is a steady change, so the readings climb or fall along a slope. [[Noise]] is the random scatter you met in the swarm. One reading tells you little, because noise moves every reading. With insulation resistance, the trend over time is what really matters. A fall warns of problems coming.[^2]

The swarm throws the order away. Lay the readings out in turn, and the order comes back. You have laid a line of best fit by eye before. Here the screen fits the straight line that sits closest to all the readings at once. Its slope measures the drift per reading. Say the line climbs 0.008 V per 10 readings. Across fifty readings it climbs about 0.04 V. Now the surprise. With no drift at all, the line still leans a little. Each batch's random errors happen to sit a little higher at one end. The line follows them, because it fits whatever readings it gets. A fresh batch leans a different way. So a fitted slope carries an uncertainty range, like any result. When that range includes zero, there may be no drift at all.[^3] A drift bigger than that noise leans the line the same way, batch after batch.

Two more checks help. First, runs. When each reading's noise is its own, six readings can come in 720 orders, all equally likely. One climbs all the way and one falls. So a given six run one way about 1 time in 360. That makes six in a row one way worth a look. A long record holds many sixes, though, so chance gives one now and then. Some rules use six and some use seven, so the number is a choice. Second, compare like with like. Insulation resistance falls as insulation warms. As a rule of thumb, it halves for each 10 °C warmer.[^4] So correct every test to one temperature, or a warm test day can look like a fault.

Last, two strings can rise and fall together without one driving the other. How closely they line up is their [[correlation]]. It runs from +1 for a perfect rising line, through 0, to −1 for a perfect falling one. A close line-up can come from a cause, from a shared cause such as the air, or from chance. It does not say which. To show a cause, change one thing yourself and watch the other.

**Judge a trend over many readings in the order taken. Noise alone makes a fitted line lean a little. So trust a drift when it leans the same way batch after batch, or runs one way for longer than chance usually gives.**

analogy.text: Think of judging the tide from a harbour wall. Each wave runs up the wall to a different height. So one wave tells you little. Watch the marks for half an hour, though, and their middle creeps up or down. The waves are the noise. The creep is the drift. Watch only three waves, and their marks can seem to climb while the tide stands still.
analogy.breaks: Waves come in a rough rhythm. Noise in readings has none. The tide also follows a curve on a timetable. A straight line fits it only for a short stretch. A drift in equipment keeps no timetable. It can speed up or stop.

practice.text:
- Take each reading the same way each time: the same connections, test voltage and time on test, and the same meter if you can.
- Note the temperature. Correct insulation resistance to one temperature, such as 20 °C, before you compare.
- Plot the readings in the order taken. Insulation resistance changes by factors, so plot it on a scale by factors.
- Judge the trend across many readings, not this one against the last.
- First find the SD of repeat readings. Then ask whether a change is bigger than that noise.
- Look for runs. Six in a row one way is worth a look.
- Read a trend line only across the readings you have. Past the last one, wear can speed up, slow or stop.
- Before you blame one thing for another, look for something that moves both. To test a cause, change one thing and watch.

**Rule of thumb:** when readings form a bell, each honest reading lands within 2 SD of the mean about 95% of the time.[^1] So two honest readings 2 SD apart are ordinary.

**Worked example:** last year a circuit's Zs read 0.80 Ω. This year it reads 0.82 Ω. Say repeat readings on it have an SD of 0.01 Ω. Each honest reading lands within 0.02 Ω of the mean about 95% of the time. So two readings 0.02 Ω apart are ordinary noise. Now say five yearly readings run 0.80, 0.81, 0.83, 0.84 and 0.86 Ω. Each was taken the same way, at a similar temperature. Each is higher than the last. Five readings can come in 120 orders, and only one climbs all the way. So pure noise does that about 1 time in 120. That is worth a look at the circuit's joints and connections.

**Common mistakes**
- Calling a drift from two readings.
- Reading a lean in a fitted line as a drift without checking fresh readings.
- Comparing tests taken at different temperatures without correcting them.
- Running a trend line forward to predict a failure date.
- Treating six in a row as a law rather than a choice.
- Reading a close line-up as proof that one thing drives the other.
- Saying a cause can never be shown, when you can change one thing and watch.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the best-fit line still leaning a little, and a different way each time, when you drop fresh batches with no drift set.

checks.label: A normal distribution with k = 2 gives an interval with a coverage probability of approximately 95%: with no drift, the lean of a best-fit line from the rule on screen has an SD of about 0.003 V per 10 readings, so 2 SDs is about 0.006 V, and of 1,000 simulated batches about 95% lean by less than that

When zero lies in the confidence interval, the true slope may be zero, no effect: the batch whose line leans +0.003 V per 10 readings with no drift has a range of its slope ± 2 standard errors that holds zero; with a drift of 0.010 V per 10 readings that range leaves zero out in most batches

What really matters is the trend in readings over a time period, showing lessening resistance: corrected to 20 °C, the opening string of sixteen tests falls along a best-fit line by about 10^−0.02 a test (about 4.5%), and its last seven each read lower than the one before; as measured, its longest run is just 3; and a run down of six or more is common in such strings

Worked by hand: six readings come in 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 720 orders and a given six run one way 1 time in 360; four come in 24 and three coin tosses give 1 in 8; five come in 120; 49 ÷ 10 = 4.9 lots, so 0.008 V per 10 climbs 0.0392 V, about 0.04 V; 300 MΩ at 30 °C is 600 MΩ at 20 °C; the largest drift is 0.001 V a reading. From the rule: the opening batch leans +0.003 V per 10 readings with no drift and its first fresh batch −0.003 V, the other way, its longest run 5; screen 4's batch reads +0.008 V at that drift and climbs 0.04 V; 3 to 5 is the longest run in about 98% of noisy batches, and the largest drift moves the average run by under 0.2; the creeping order has the same fifty values; the two strings line up at +0.91 with the air swinging ±3 °C and about 0 with it steady

Drawn true, and each puzzle hidden until answered: settled, the fulcrum sits under the mean and the mean's value clears every bead and the pegs; in 60 batches at every drift no two beads touch, each keeps inside its room, none is under r 3.2, and a reading past the scale sits in its overflow pile; turned onto its side the swarm lies level with the time view, against the right edge, and the best-fit line passes through the mean point, at every drift; the fade deepens outward on each side, its deepest 3:1 against the page and its palest still seen; each puzzle accepts one right answer of three, and before it nothing gives the answer away; a right answer brings each in; every demonstration settles within 5 s, and every answer within 2.5 s

applied.problem: "A real drift leans the line the same way, batch after batch" fails for small drifts: at 0.001 to 0.003 V per 10 readings the noise lean (about ±0.006 V) still tips 15 to 37% of batches the other way. Narrowed to a drift bigger than the noise.

Screen 5 repeats the same over-general claim, false at the slider's low settings; and screen 9's "the longest run down reaches six or more" holds in only about 60% of fresh batches of the stated rule, so it becomes "often".

The last common mistake, "Saying a line-up can never show a cause", read alone contradicts the explanation (a line-up on its own does not say which cause); the real mistake is saying a cause can never be shown, when changing one thing and watching can show it.
